before.quote: The tariff keeps our workshops busy and our wages steady. The other fellow talks of cutting duties, but that's a path to ruin for men in trade like us.
before.reason: Walter Lawson is a merchant or office worker in Illinois—a man of commercial interests who would read business news and follow tariff and currency questions closely. The recent dispatches on gold and silver coinage, falling imports, and weak wheat prices would concern a man of his class; Blaine's commitment to protective tariffs and sound money, proven by the administration's handling of the Treasury, aligns with the economic stability his livelihood depends on.

after.quote: The Republicans have kept our industries and wages strong these past twenty years. I worry about their talk of cutting the tariff, but the Democrat seems to want to shake things up too much.
after.reason: Walter Lawson is a white male householder in Illinois, eligible to vote. He has been exposed to recent economic and political news, particularly regarding tariffs, labor, and the Treasury surplus. The Republican administration's commitment to protective tariffs and labor protections aligns with interests typical of a clerk or small-store owner in this era, though the Democrat's anti-corruption message and tariff revision platform hold some appeal.

before.quote: The tariff keeps our wages up and our jobs safe from cheap foreign goods and labor. That's what matters to a working man like me.
before.reason: Ernest Reed works in a mill or related industry in Massachusetts, where the Republican Blaine strongly emphasizes tariff protection for American wages and workers—a direct economic interest for a working man. The recent Independent Statesman piece praising the Republican nominee as 'the wisest friend of the laborer' and 'the most eminent representative of the American system of protection' aligns with protectionist sentiment common among industrial workers in Massachusetts.

after.quote: The Republican's been good for working men like me in the mills. He stands for the tariff that keeps our wages up, not like the other fellow wants to cut it down.
after.reason: Ernest Reed is a mill worker in Massachusetts whose wages depend on industrial protection. Blaine explicitly promises tariff duties to protect American industries and workers' wages, directly aligning with Reed's economic interests as a laboring man in a protected industry.

before.quote: I cannot vote myself, but my husband will attend to it tomorrow. We shall see what the election brings.
before.reason: Helen Dawson is a woman living in Indiana in 1884, and women are legally barred from voting for president in this state and throughout the United States at this time.

after.quote: I follow the news well enough, but the voting is not for the likes of me. My husband will cast his ballot tomorrow.
after.reason: Helen Dawson is a woman living in Indiana in 1884, and women cannot vote for president in the state. She is therefore prohibited by law from casting a ballot regardless of her preferences or engagement with the election.

before.quote: I can't vote myself, but my husband will be going to the polls tomorrow. I hope he chooses wisely for all of us.

after.quote: I cannot vote myself, but my husband will go to the polls tomorrow to cast his ballot.

before.quote: The Republican's been in office long enough to have earned my vote on this tariff business. My wages depend on American factories staying strong, not being undercut by cheap foreign labor.
before.reason: Samuel Porter works in a mill, shop, mine or railroad—occupations where tariff protection of American industry and opposition to contract labor directly affect wages and job security. Blaine's platform of protective tariffs, opposition to imported contract labor, and labor protections aligns with his material interests as a working man in 1884.

after.quote: I'm thinking the Republican fellow's got the right idea on keeping up wages with tariffs, but this corruption business troubles me some. I'll likely vote for him, though it's not a settled thing.
after.reason: Samuel Porter works in a mill or railroad in New York and would benefit from the Republican candidate's protective tariff and labor protections, but the Democratic candidate's anti-corruption message and tax-cutting platform have genuine appeal. The recent clerical gathering's welcome for the administration candidate suggests some community support.

before.quote: I reckon the Republican has done right by working men and farmers with the tariff. Though the other fellow talks a good game about cleaning up corruption in Washington.
before.reason: James Hayes is a Tennessee farmer who would naturally align with the Republican administration's pro-tariff stance to protect domestic agriculture and industry, and its labor reforms appeal to rural workers. However, the Democratic candidate's anti-corruption platform and treasury reform message have some appeal, and Hayes may be uncertain about voting at all given the volatile political climate.

after.quote: The Republican's been good to us farmers with the tariff. I'll vote to keep things as they are rather than risk my livelihood to some Democrat's notion of free trade.
after.reason: Hayes is a rural Tennessee farmer whose livelihood depends on protective tariffs for American agriculture and labor. Blaine's platform of tariff protection and opposition to contract labor aligns with his economic interests. The Democratic nominee's call for tariff reduction threatens the farming economy Hayes depends on.

before.quote: I cannot vote—the law doesn't allow it. But I wish my husband would pay attention to what labor has won these past two years.

before.quote: The man coming in promises to undo the laws that keep us from organizing and to stop the convict labor undercutting our wages. That matters more to me than talk about tariffs.
before.reason: Harry Tate is a mill or railroad worker in Illinois whose wages depend on steady employment and fair conditions. Cleveland explicitly pledges to repeal laws restricting labor, let labor organizations incorporate, and oppose convict and imported contract labor—reforms that directly address the working man's grievances. Blaine, the administration's candidate, has held power through economic cycles that have favored capital over labor, and Tate has read of significant recent labor victories achieved only by persistent appeals against the incumbent party's resistance.

after.quote: The men at the mill say the administration's done right by labor these past years. I'll stick with them tomorrow.
after.reason: Harry Tate is a wage worker in Illinois whose household depends on mill or railroad income. The brief shows labor has won six legislative victories in the last two years and Blaine explicitly backs labor protections—national labor bureau, eight-hour law, opposition to contract labor—while Cleveland merely pledges to repeal labor restrictions without specifying what he would enact instead. Tate would likely vote and favor the administration's candidate.

before.quote: The Republicans have had long enough at the helm. We need lower tariffs and an honest reckoning, not a swollen Treasury and endless taxes on working folks like us.
before.reason: Frank Baker is a tradesman or store clerk in Tennessee whose livelihood depends on commercial activity and fair pricing. He has read of prohibition's economic benefits to merchants and workers, and he favors the opposition party's pledge to cut the tariff and reduce the Treasury surplus, which aligns with his interest in lower costs and less government intervention.

after.quote: The tariff keeps our wages up and our shops busy. That other fellow talks about cutting taxes, but we need those duties to protect what we've got here.
after.reason: Frank Baker is a white male store or office worker in Tennessee eligible to vote. His recent exposure to prohibition arguments and labor protections rhetoric suggests interests in reform, but the incumbent party's defense of protective tariffs, opposition to contract labor, and civil service merit system align with his likely commercial interests and Tennessee's Republican leanings during Reconstruction's aftermath.
